extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards derived from Aristotle's Poetics (with editorial notes) for composing and judging poetry, especially tragedy: its elements, unity, plot-structure, character, diction, and the aims (catharsis, universality) of poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the organising principle
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ (μέμησις) the common principle of the Arts of Poetry, Music, Dancing, Painting, and Sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All these arts are modes of imitation; recognising mimesis as the fundamental principle frames how to assess medium, objects, and manner of representation. Use this to ask what is being imitated and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Medium of Imitation is Rhythm, Language, and ‘Harmony’ (or Melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different arts employ different media (e.g. flute/lyre use harmony and rhythm alone; dancing uses rhythm; poetry uses language ± rhythm ± harmony). Choose and control your medium deliberately; the medium shapes what can be imitated and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (higher/lower types)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Objects of Imitation. Higher or lower types are represented in all the Imitative Arts. In Poetry this is the basis of the distinction between Tragedy and Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to represent men as better than in real life, worse, or as they are; that choice defines genre (tragedy tends to idealize, comedy to degrade) and affects tone and ethical portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs dramatic presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manner of Imitation. Poetry may be in form either dramatic narrative, pure narrative (including lyric poetry), or pure drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet may imitate by narration (speaking in authorial voice or another persona) or by presenting characters acting before us; the manner determines immediacy and dramatic effect and should match the aims of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Six elements in Tragedy : three external, —namely, Spectacular Presentment (ὁ τῆς ὄψεως κόσμος or ὄψι), Lyrical Song (μελοποιία), Diction (λέξις) ; three internal,— namely, Plot (μῦθος), Character (ἦθος), and Thought (διάνοια).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is primary; Character and Thought follow. Evaluate a tragedy by assessing each element and how well external (spectacle, song, diction) integrates with internal elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot, or the representation of the action, is of primary importance ; Character and Thought come next in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the action first: the plot should drive tragic emotions and be the main determiner of the work's success. Avoid letting character or spectacle alone determine the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole and of adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot has a coherent beginning, middle, and end and is neither trivial nor sprawling; parts should cohere into an organic whole with appropriate scale for the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (primary unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Plot consists not in Unity of Hero, but in Unity of Action. The parts must be organically connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise a single, coherent action or causal chain. Avoid unrelated subplots or episodic diversions that break the organic connection of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic (dramatic) truth vs historical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic Unity can be attained only by the observance of Poetic as distinct from Historic Truth; Poetry is an expression of the Universal, History of the Particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess incidents by their poetic probability/necessity rather than literal factuality. Choose events that reveal universal human truths even if not empirically exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of probable or necessary sequence as applied to the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot incidents should follow from each other by necessity or credible probability; avoid chance or arbitrary events that undermine unity and believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Tragic effects depend on the combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for outcomes that feel both necessary (earned) and surprising; craft reversals and recognitions so that they are unforeseen yet logically inevitable in retrospect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots; peripeteia, anagnorisis, pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of Simple (ἁπλοῖ) and Complex (πεπλεγμένοι) Plots. Reversal of the Situation (περιπέτεια), Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις), and Tragic or disastrous Incident (πάθος) defined and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complex plots (reversal and recognition) to achieve cathartic impact; know the structural roles of peripeteia and anagnorisis and place them to maximize organic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘quantitative parts’ (μέρη κατὰ τὸ ποσόν) of Tragedy defined :—Prologue, Episode, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the play into its requisite parts; even if some chapters are interpolated editorially, recognise conventional divisions to organise pacing and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune and character as requisites for tragic action
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes Tragic Action. The change of fortune and the character of the hero as a requisite to an ideal Tragedy. The unhappy ending more truly tragic than the ‘poetic justice’ which is in favour with a popular audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the protagonist undergoes a meaningful reversal tied to character and action; avoid contrived moral tidyings that make tragedy merely satisfy popular justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must spring from the Plot itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself. To produce them by Scenery or Spectacular effect is entirely against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicit emotional responses via organic plot development and character situations rather than relying on spectacle, shock effects, or stagecraft alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: ethical portraiture and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of Character (as the manifestation of moral purpose) in Tragedy. Requisites of ethical portraiture. The rule of necessity or probability applicable to Character as to Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should act consistently with their moral purpose and probabilities; character actions must be motivated and necessary to the plot, not arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deus ex Machina is improper
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘Deus ex Machina’ (a passage out of place here).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid convenient supernatural or external devices that resolve the plot without organic development; they violate unity and poetic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical compositional rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules for the Tragic Poet : (1) To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself in order to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae. (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enter into the characters by embodiment or rehearsal; outline the whole action first, then compose episodes. These steps help maintain unity and emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further practical rules: complication, dénouement, variety, chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: Further rules for the Tragic Poet : (1) To be careful about the Complication (δέσις) and Dénouement (λύσις) of the Plot, especially the Dénouement. (2) To unite, if possible, varied forms of poetic excellence. (3) Not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry. (4) To make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay special attention to how knots are tied and resolved; balance forms (song, speech, spectacle); avoid epic-length digressions; integrate chorus and lyric elements so they serve the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) and Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (διάνοια), or the Intellectual element, and Diction in Tragedy. Thought is revealed in the dramatic speeches composed according to the rules of Rhetoric. Diction falls largely within the domain of the Art of Delivery, rather than of Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speeches to reveal ideas and argument; apply rhetorical principles. Choose diction appropriate to delivery and dramatic context; balance elevation with clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: metaphor and balance of elevation and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic Diction. The words and modes of speech admissible in Poetry: including Metaphor, in particular. How Poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors and elevated language, but not at the cost of intelligibility. Aim for language that is both elevated and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: shared unity of action and distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic Poetry. It agrees with Tragedy in Unity of Action ... The points of difference are enumerated and illustrated,—namely, (1) the length of the poem; (2) the metre ; (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epic vs tragic works, preserve unity of action but adjust for length, metre, and techniques that make extraordinary events feel plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth and exclusion of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry excludes the rule of Chance ... Poetic Truth: Poetry is not a reproduction of empirical fact: the ‘probabilities and ‘possibilities’ of Poetry contrasted with those of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on random chance to resolve plot; instead base events on poetic probability and possibility that reveal universal aspects of human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of tragedy: catharsis (clarifying of emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic Katharsis of pity and fear ... The Katharsis implies not only an emotional relief but a softening or clarifying of emotion. How this clarifying process is effected ... The Katharsis theory connected with the general core of Poetry as a representation of the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure plot and character so that pity and fear lead to catharsis—an emotional clarification or purification—rather than mere sensational release. Consider the conditions under which cathartic treatment is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic unities (action, time, place) and their hierarchical value
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Unity of Action’ is the primary Unity. ‘Unity of Time’: the prevailing practice of the Greek stage... afterwards made into a rule of dramatic art. ‘Unity of Place’ nowhere mentioned in Aristotle; Idealisation of Time and Place. The higher law of ‘Unity of Action’ often intrinsic to the minor Unities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise unity of action above rigid adherence to time/place unities: unity of time and place may be idealised or adapted, but should not sacrifice the organic unity of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal type of protagonist is deduced by Aristotle ... The several types of excluded characters: blameless goodness; signal villainy. Aristotle’s ideal protagonist: meaning of ἁμαρτία.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a protagonist whose moral complexity (hamartia) allows for a believable reversal that elicits pity and fear; avoid heroes who are purely flawless or purely monstrous in ways that make tragic collision impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot vs Character emphasis (action over ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis with which Aristotle subordinates ἦθος to ‘Action’ ... Plot (μῦθος) or Action ... is the primary element according to Aristotle; ‘Ethos’ and ‘Dianoia’ constitute Character in its largest sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, assess whether character serves the action and whether action reveals character; modern drama may lay increased stress on character, but action should still dominate in a classical tragic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s mode: universalising by representing the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: The Generalising Power of Comedy ... The pleasure of the ludicrous ... Aristotle selects Comedy as an example of the universalising suits of Poetry. Comedy, in its purely sportive form, creates personified ideals; Tragedy, idealised persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comic composition, aim to universalise by portraying types and the ludicrous; distinguish comic idealisation (personified ideals) from tragic idealisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of poetry: instincts of imitation and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychologically, Poetry may be traced to two causes, the instinct of Imitation, and the instinct of ‘Harmony’ and Rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or teaching poetry, leverage natural human instincts—imitation and responsiveness to rhythm/harmony—to engage readers and produce pleasure in learning and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and morality: aesthetic primacy with moral considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes the educational from the aesthetic function of Poetry: his critical estimates of Poetry rest on purely aesthetic grounds. Yet some of his rules indicate a sense of moral and ethical excellence; e.g. tragic characters must be σπουδαῖοι.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetry primarily by aesthetic criteria but acknowledge moral dimensions when they bear on character plausibility and the work’s ethical portraiture; avoid didacticism that overrides aesthetic aims.
